**In Praise of Slow Wonder**

I want to begin with a window. Not a metaphorical window, not a window into the soul or any of that, but a real, slightly smudged kitchen window on an ordinary morning.

Outside it, light is doing what it has done every morning for about four and a half billion years, which is to arrive. It comes slanting through leaves, it pools on the countertop, it catches the steam rising off a mug and for half a second turns something completely ordinary — hot water and ground beans — into something that looks choreographed. I have always loved that first hour of the day because the world hasn't yet asked you to be efficient. The emails are there, of course, waiting like patient dogs by the door, but they haven't started barking yet. The news is waiting too. For a little while you can just stand there and watch dust motes turn slowly in a sunbeam and feel, with a kind of embarrassing sincerity, that this is enough. That this has always been enough, and we just forget.

If I could write freely about anything, and I can, I want to write about that forgetting and remembering. About attention, and time, and the very strange luck of being conscious in a universe that doesn't require consciousness at all. About how we live surrounded by miracles we have filed away under "normal."

Consider attention. Everyone talks about it now as if it were a resource, like oil or lithium, something to be mined and traded. And in a way it is. Your attention is the most valuable thing you own, not because companies will pay for it — though they will — but because it is literally what your life is made of. You do not experience the world directly; you experience what you pay attention to. Two people can walk down the same street and live in entirely different cities. One notices the way the old brick building has been repointed with slightly mismatched mortar, the pigeons arguing over a french fry, the kid on a scooter practicing the same turn over and over until he gets it right and throws both arms up like he just won the Olympics. The other notices nothing, because their mind was replaying an argument from three days ago and rehearsing an argument for three days from now. Same street, same ten minutes, different lives.

I think about this a lot because we have built a civilization that is exquisitely good at stealing attention and not very good at teaching us what to do with it once we get it back. The phone in your pocket is a marvel — it contains more computing power than NASA had when we put people on the Moon, it gives you instant access to almost the entire archive of human knowledge and art and silliness — and it is also a slot machine that you carry into the bathroom. Both things are true. It's not that technology is bad; it's that it is exquisitely tuned to our novelty bias. We are descendants of primates who survived because they noticed the rustle in the grass. Of course we look when something dings. Of course we scroll. To pay sustained attention now feels almost rebellious. To read a novel for two hours without checking anything, to watch a pot of water boil just to watch it, to listen to a friend without planning what you'll say next — these feel like radical acts.

And yet attention is a skill, which means it can be trained, and it can also atrophy. I love the idea that wonder is not something you find, it's something you practice. You don't need to go to Iceland to see the northern lights, though if you can, please do. You can practice on a Tuesday. Look closer. Look longer. The naturalist Diane Ackerman wrote that with a microscope you can see that a drop of pond water is a jungle. With sustained looking, the same is true of almost anything. A face. A sentence. A cup of tea. The trick is to stay with it past the point where your brain says "okay, got it, categorized, moving on," and into the second and third seeing, where texture appears.

Take something as unglamorous as a library. I mean a real public library, with that particular smell of old paper and carpet cleaner and possibility. Every library is a kind of time machine and a kind of afterlife. The people who wrote those books are mostly gone. Their worries about rent and illness and whether they were loved enough — gone with them. But their best thinking, their most careful sentences, remain, shelved and waiting for a stranger decades or centuries later to open them and think, "Oh, you felt this too?" That is astonishing if you stop to think about it. We have invented a way for minds to touch across time.

I used to wander the stacks with no agenda, pulling down books by their spines, reading first paragraphs like tasting samples. That's how I discovered that you can learn navigation from Polynesian voyagers who read waves like text, that octopuses have three hearts and can taste with their arms, that medieval monks doodled grumpy cats in the margins of manuscripts and complained about the cold exactly the way we complain about office air conditioning. A library tells you, quietly and without fanfare, that you are not the first person to be confused, and you won't be the last, and that is strangely comforting. The internet can give you answers faster, but a library gives you something else: serendipity. You go looking for a book on gardening and you come home with a memoir by a beekeeper and a new obsession with soil. Algorithms give you more of what you already wanted. Shelves give you what you didn't know you needed.

That same serendipity is everywhere in the natural world, if we let ourselves look. We live, at this moment, on the only known planet with life — with hummingbirds that fly backwards and moths that navigate by moonlight and fungi that connect trees into vast underground networks sometimes called the wood wide web. When it rains in a pine forest, the air fills with petrichor and phytoncides, chemicals that actually lower human stress hormones. We evolved in this. Our nervous systems expect birdsong and moving water and dappled light. No wonder we feel better after a walk in the woods than after an hour scrolling. It's not romanticism; it's biology remembering itself.

I think one of the saddest subtle shifts of modern life is that we have moved from being participants in nature to being viewers of it. We watch documentaries in stunning 8K about coral reefs while the actual reefs bleach. We keep nature as a screensaver. But the real thing is embarrassingly close and persistently strange. Even in a city: watch pigeons. People dismiss them as rats with wings, but pigeons can recognize themselves in mirrors, navigate hundreds of miles home using Earth's magnetic field and infrasound, and court each other with a dance that is, if you watch long enough, genuinely tender. Or watch ants on a sidewalk crack carrying crumbs ten times their weight, forming living bridges with their bodies. Or simply look up at a tree in autumn and try to comprehend what is happening: a living organism is dismantling its solar panels, pulling the green chlorophyll back into its branches, revealing yellows and reds that were there all along, then sealing off the leaf with a little scar and letting it fall. It does this every year without anxiety. It trusts spring.

There is a lesson in that, though I am wary of turning nature into a self-help book. Nature is not always kind or wise; it is also parasites and wildfires and extinctions. But it is patient in a way we rarely are. It works on timescales that make our deadlines look absurd. A redwood can live two thousand years. A stone in a riverbed may have been tumbling smooth since before humans had language. When I feel frantic — and I do, often — I try to borrow some of that deep time. I put my hand on an old tree trunk and think: you were here before my grandparents were born and you will, if we are lucky and careful, be here after I'm gone. My urgent inbox is not the whole story.

Speaking of stories, let's talk about people. Because for all the beauty of forests and stars, the most reliably astonishing thing I have ever encountered is other humans. Not humanity in the abstract — humanity in the abstract is exhausting — but specific humans in specific moments.

Like the time I saw a bus driver in the rain wait an extra thirty seconds for an elderly woman running with a plastic bag over her head, and then greet her like an old friend, and the whole bus seemed to exhale. Or the neighbor who leaves extra zucchini from his garden on everyone's doorstep in August with a note that says "please help, they won't stop." Or the night-shift nurses who remember how you take your tea even though you only met them yesterday during the worst week of your life. These are small kindnesses, unrecorded, unoptimized for engagement. They will never go viral. They are the actual social network, the one that holds when everything else fails.

We underestimate how much we affect each other in passing. A study once showed that even brief positive interactions with strangers — a smile, a short chat with a barista — significantly increase well-being. And yet in many cities we have trained ourselves to look past each other, to treat shared spaces as inconveniences between private destinations. Earbuds in, eyes down. I understand it; the world can be overstimulating, and solitude is precious. But there is a particular joy in allowing yourself to be interruptible. To ask the taxi driver how long he's been driving and actually listen. To compliment someone's laugh. To let a conversation with no purpose take up ten minutes you had allocated to productivity and discover that those ten minutes are the part of the day you remember.

Language is part of this magic. That we can make small noises with our mouths and transfer a thought from one brain to another is so common we forget how uncanny it is. I say "I had a dream where I was back in my childhood house but all the rooms were full of water and my dog could talk," and suddenly you can see it. You have never been in my dream, but now a version of it lives in you too. Words are telepathy with extra steps. And music is even stranger — organized air vibrations that can make thousands of strangers cry at the same time or dance with people they just met. Every culture humans have ever made has sung to its babies and danced to mark seasons and mourned with laments. Before we had writing, we had rhythm.

I sometimes wonder what future archaeologists will make of us. They will dig through our landfills and find billions of plastic bottles and fast-fashion tags and dead phones, and they might conclude we worshipped convenience. I hope they also find libraries and love letters and instruments with worn frets where fingers played the same chords ten thousand times. I hope they find evidence that we also worshipped beauty, even if we were bad at protecting it.

That brings me to memory and time, because writing freely for a while inevitably curves back to time. Time is the thing we all have in common and understand the least. Physicists will tell you it may be an illusion, that past and future might exist simultaneously in some block universe, but your body knows better when you are waiting for test results or watching a child grow. Time feels fast when you are happy and slow when you are bored and impossibly strange when you are grieving.

We talk about saving time as if time were money, but time is not money. Money you can store. Time you can only spend, and you spend it whether you choose to or not, at a rate of sixty seconds per minute. The only choice is what you spend it *on*, and more importantly, what you spend it *with*. Attention, again. A life is not measured by how many things you optimized; it's measured by how many moments you were actually there for.

Nostalgia complicates this. We remember the past as better than it was because memory edits out the waiting rooms and the mosquito bites and keeps the golden light on the lake. That's okay. Memory is not a documentary; it's a story we tell ourselves to make sense of who we've become. But I worry when nostalgia becomes a place to live instead of a place to visit. The past is a lovely house, but you can't move back in. The present, for all its mess, is the only place where you can act. The future is unwritten, which is terrifying and also the best news possible.

If you want a practical exercise in time travel, try this: write a letter to yourself to be opened in a year. Describe an ordinary day in ridiculous detail — what you ate for breakfast, what song was stuck in your head, what you were worried about, what the sky looked like. Seal it. Forget about it. When you open it, you will be amazed at two things: how much has changed, and how much is exactly the same. You will feel tenderness for the person you were, who didn't know how things would turn out. That tenderness is worth cultivating. We are always future ancestors to ourselves.

Boredom deserves a defense here, too. We have pathologized boredom, treated it as a problem to be solved with content. But boredom is not empty; it's fallow. It's the field resting before planting. Every creative person I admire talks about the importance of doing nothing — staring out train windows, taking long showers, going for walks without podcasts. The mind needs unstructured time to make unexpected connections. When you are bored, your brain switches to what neuroscientists call the default mode network, which is involved in memory, imagination, and thinking about other people. In other words, when you think you're doing nothing, you're doing some of the most human thinking there is.

I remember being a kid on long car rides before tablets, watching telephone poles flick past, making up games with license plates, getting so bored I started narrating the inner lives of cows in fields. It felt like torture at the time. Now I suspect it was education. I learned how to entertain myself, which is another way of saying I learned how to be alone without being lonely. That's a skill many adults have lost. We reach for the phone in every elevator, every checkout line, every red light. We have filled every crack of stillness with stimulation, and then we wonder why we feel fragmented.

What if we reclaimed some of that stillness? Not in a grand, move-to-a-cabin-in-the-woods way — though tempting — but in small, doable ways. Drink your coffee without doing anything else, just to taste it. Take a walk around the block and leave the phone at home, to see what happens. Sit on a bench and watch people. Let your mind wander and see where it goes without yanking it back. At first it will feel itchy. That's withdrawal. Stay a little longer. Something will surface — an idea, a memory, a feeling you had been outrunning. That is your inner life knocking. Let it in.

And then there is the night sky, which is my favorite cure for both arrogance and despair. On a clear night far from city lights, you can see with your naked eyes a few thousand stars. Each one is a sun. Many have planets. The light from some of those stars left before humans built the pyramids. You are seeing ancient history with your eyeballs. And that is just the visible part. Beyond that are galaxies, hundreds of billions of them, each with hundreds of billions of stars. The scale is so large it breaks the brain's ability to visualize, which is precisely why it's good for us. It puts the argument you had on the internet into perspective.

But the night sky is not just humbling; it's also intimate. The atoms in your body — the carbon in your cells, the iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones — were forged in stars that exploded billions of years ago. You are, quite literally, stardust that has temporarily organized itself into a form capable of wondering about stars. The universe, after 13.8 billion years of expansion and cooling and collapsing, has produced a creature on a small blue planet who can look up and feel awe. That feels like the point, if there is a point. Not to conquer the universe, but to witness it.

I think that's why I love both science and art, and why I refuse to choose between them. Science tells me how the light gets here; art tells me what it feels like when it lands on my face. Science can explain that a robin's song is territorial signaling shaped by evolution; poetry can capture why it makes me stop on a February morning with my heart full. Both are true. We need explanations and we need meanings, and they are not the same thing.

If I were allowed to prescribe one thing for the collective malaise I sense — that low hum of anxiety so many of us carry — it wouldn't be a productivity hack or a morning routine, though those have their place. It would be more moments of unproductive wonder. Watch the moon rise. Learn the names of three trees on your street. Memorize a poem just because you like how it sounds in your mouth. Cook something slow. Write something by hand. Call someone you miss for no reason. Lie on the floor and listen to an entire album without doing anything else. These are inefficient uses of time, which is exactly why they are valuable. They remind you that you are a person, not a project.

I also want to say something about grief, because any honest long reflection has to make room for it. To love anything in this world — a person, a pet, a place, a season of life — is to agree in advance to lose it. That is the terrible price, and we pay it over and over. And yet we keep loving. Why? Because the alternative — to love nothing to avoid loss — is a different kind of loss, quieter but total. Grief is not the opposite of love; it's the receipt. It proves the transaction was real.

If you are grieving now, I am sorry. I don't have wisdom that will fix it. I only know that grief moves like weather, not like a task to complete. Some days will be clear. Some will knock you sideways with a smell in a grocery store. Be gentle with yourself. Talk to people who knew what you lost. Keep the ridiculous rituals — the birthday candle, the walk you used to take together. Over time, the sharpest edges soften, not because you forget, but because you grow around the absence, the way a tree grows around a fence.

And if you are in a good season — truly good, not performatively good for social media — please notice it while you're in it. We have a habit of recognizing happiness only in retrospect. "Remember that summer?" we say, when we could have said, on an ordinary Tuesday in the middle of that summer, "This is good. I'm happy right now." Try saying it out loud, even if you feel silly. It anchors the moment. Future you will thank present you for pausing to mark it.

As I write this, I am aware of how lucky I am to be able to string sentences together and have someone, somewhere, read them. Writing is an act of faith. You send words out into the void not knowing who will catch them. Maybe you're reading this in the morning with coffee, like me at my window. Maybe it's late at night and you can't sleep. Maybe you stumbled here by accident and stayed out of curiosity. Whoever you are, I wonder what your ordinary miracles are. What small thing anchors your day? What sound immediately makes you feel at home? What do you know how to do with your hands?

I hope you get to do more of that. I hope you get to be bored and be amazed in equal measure. I hope you look up more often — at clouds, at ceilings in old buildings, at the faces of people you love when they're not performing, just being. I hope you forgive yourself for the years you spent distracted; we all did, the distraction was engineered by very smart people. Starting now, starting today, you can practice coming back. Attention is like breath in meditation: you will lose it a thousand times, and you can return a thousand times. The returning is the practice.

The light has moved off my countertop now. The morning is getting on with itself. Soon I will join it, answer the waiting messages, do the necessary chores, participate in the beautiful, flawed, ongoing project of being a person among people. But for a moment longer I want to stay here in this quiet, with the steam and the dust motes, with the feeling that life is not a problem to be solved but a gift to be noticed.

There is a line by the poet Mary Oliver that I return to constantly: "Attention is the beginning of devotion." I think she is right. What we pay attention to, we come to love. What we love, we protect. And what we protect, endures. So perhaps the most important, most political, most spiritual thing we can do is also the simplest: to look, really look, at the world we've been given, and to find it — despite everything, because of everything — worth our wonder.

If you've read this far, thank you for lending me your attention, that precious, life-stuff material. I promise I don't take it lightly. Now go outside if you can, even for five minutes. Find one small thing you would have missed if you had been hurrying. A crack in the sidewalk where something green is growing anyway. A shadow doing something interesting. The particular blue of today's sky, which will never, in the entire history of the universe, happen exactly this way again.

Notice it. That's all. That's everything.

Drink your coffee without doing anything else, just to taste it. Take a walk around the block and leave the phone at home, to see what happens. Sit on a bench and watch people. Let your mind wander and see where it goes without yanking it back. At first it will feel itchy. That's withdrawal. Stay a little longer. Something will surface — an idea, a memory, a feeling you had been outrunning. That is your inner life knocking. Let it in.

And then there is the night sky, which is my favorite cure for both arrogance and despair. On a clear night far from city lights, you can see with your naked eyes a few thousand stars. Each one is a sun. Many have planets. The light from some of those stars left before humans built the pyramids. You are seeing ancient history with your eyeballs. And that is just the visible part. Beyond that are galaxies, hundreds of billions of them, each with hundreds of billions of stars. The scale is so large it breaks the brain's ability to visualize, which is precisely why it's good for us. It puts the argument you had on the internet into perspective.

But the night sky is not just humbling; it's also intimate. The atoms in your body — the carbon in your cells, the iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones — were forged in stars that exploded billions of years ago. You are, quite literally, stardust that has temporarily organized itself into a form capable of wondering about stars. The universe, after 13.8 billion years of expansion and cooling and collapsing, has produced a creature on a small blue planet who can look up and feel awe. That feels like the point, if there is a point. Not to conquer the universe, but to witness it.

I think that's why I love both science and art, and why I refuse to choose between them. Science tells me how the light gets here; art tells me what it feels like when it lands on my face. Science can explain that a robin's song is territorial signaling shaped by evolution; poetry can capture why it makes me stop on a February morning with my heart full. Both are true. We need explanations and we need meanings, and they are not the same thing.

If I were allowed to prescribe one thing for the collective malaise I sense — that low hum of anxiety so many of us carry — it wouldn't be a productivity hack or a morning routine, though those have their place. It would be more moments of unproductive wonder. Watch the moon rise. Learn the names of three trees on your street. Memorize a poem just because you like how it sounds in your mouth. Cook something slow. Write something by hand. Call someone you miss for no reason. Lie on the floor and listen to an entire album without doing anything else. These are inefficient uses of time, which is exactly why they are valuable. They remind you that you are a person, not a project.

I also want to say something about grief, because any honest long reflection has to make room for it. To love anything in this world — a person, a pet, a place, a season of life — is to agree in advance to lose it. That is the terrible price, and we pay it over and over. And yet we keep loving. Why? Because the alternative — to love nothing to avoid loss — is a different kind of loss, quieter but total. Grief is not the opposite of love; it's the receipt. It proves the transaction was real.

If you are grieving now, I am sorry. I don't have wisdom that will fix it. I only know that grief moves like weather, not like a task to complete. Some days will be clear. Some will knock you sideways with a smell in a grocery store. Be gentle with yourself. Talk to people who knew what you lost. Keep the ridiculous rituals — the birthday candle, the walk you used to take together. Over time, the sharpest edges soften, not because you forget, but because you grow around the absence, the way a tree grows around a fence.

And if you are in a good season — truly good, not performatively good for social media — please notice it while you're in it. We have a habit of recognizing happiness only in retrospect. "Remember that summer?" we say, when we could have said, on an ordinary Tuesday in the middle of that summer, "This is good. I'm happy right now." Try saying it out loud, even if you feel silly. It anchors the moment. Future you will thank present you for pausing to mark it.

As I write this, I am aware of how lucky I am to be able to string sentences together and have someone, somewhere, read them. Writing is an act of faith. You send words out into the void not knowing who will catch them. Maybe you're reading this in the morning with coffee, like me at my window. Maybe it's late at night and you can't sleep. Maybe you stumbled here by accident and stayed out of curiosity. Whoever you are, I wonder what your ordinary miracles are. What small thing anchors your day? What sound immediately makes you feel at home? What do you know how to do with your hands?

I hope you get to do more of that. I hope you get to be bored and be amazed in equal measure. I hope you look up more often — at clouds, at ceilings in old buildings, at the faces of people you love when they're not performing, just being. I hope you forgive yourself for the years you spent distracted; we all did, the distraction was engineered by very smart people. Starting now, starting today, you can practice coming back. Attention is like breath in meditation: you will lose it a thousand times, and you can return a thousand times. The returning is the practice.

The light has moved off my countertop now. The morning is getting on with itself. Soon I will join it, answer the waiting messages, do the necessary chores, participate in the beautiful, flawed, ongoing project of being a person among people. But for a moment longer I want to stay here in this quiet, with the steam and the dust motes, with the feeling that life is not a problem to be solved but a gift to be noticed.

There is a line by the poet Mary Oliver that I return to constantly: "Attention is the beginning of devotion." I think she is right. What we pay attention to, we come to love. What we love, we protect. And what we protect, endures. So perhaps the most important, most political, most spiritual thing we can do is also the simplest: to look, really look, at the world we've been given, and to find it — despite everything, because of everything — worth our wonder.

If you've read this far, thank you for lending me your attention, that precious, life-stuff material. I promise I don't take it lightly. Now go outside if you can, even for five minutes. Find one small thing you would have missed if you had been hurrying. A crack in the sidewalk where something green is growing anyway. A shadow doing something interesting. The particular blue of today's sky, which will never, in the entire history of the universe, happen exactly this way again.

Notice it. That's all. That's everything.
